question: What first drew you to studying geology?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin of interest, not a generic love of rocks or nature.

bullets: Name a concrete moment or experience, not a vague love of nature
Explain what stayed with you and why it mattered
Link it to why you now want to study it formally
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I got hooked on a school trip to a limestone gorge where our teacher pointed out ripple marks in rock that used to be a seabed, and I remember thinking the ground under my feet was basically a very slow history book. I started reading about how landscapes form after that, and I've been picking up loose rocks on every walk since. Studying geology properly means I can finally learn to read that history rather than just guess at it.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always loved rocks' with nothing more specific
Talking only about loving the outdoors with no geology content
Sounding like they haven't thought about it before the interview
followUps: What's the most interesting rock or landscape you've seen since then?

question: Why do you want to study geology here specifically, rather than at another university?
lookingFor: Research beyond rankings, tied to actual course content, facilities, or staff.

bullets: Name a specific module, field trip, lab, or research strength of the department
Connect it to a concrete interest or goal of theirs
Show they understand what's distinct about this course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course has a first-year field mapping trip built in from year one rather than year two, which matters to me because I learn geology best outside the classroom, not from a textbook. I also read about the department's work on volcanic hazard modelling, and that's the direction I think I want to specialise in. Most courses I looked at treat fieldwork as an add-on, but here it feels central, which is exactly what I want.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that would fit any geology department
Citing only league table position
Not being able to name anything specific about the course
followUps: What would you want to get out of that first field trip?

question: Was there a particular place or experience that made you want to study geology?
lookingFor: An authentic personal connection to landscape or rocks, with genuine curiosity behind it.

bullets: Describe a specific place, event, or object
Explain what question it left them with
Show ongoing curiosity beyond that one moment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My grandfather kept a drawer of fossils he'd collected as a boy near the coast, and when I was about twelve he showed me an ammonite and told me it was older than the dinosaurs. I didn't really believe him until I looked it up, and then I couldn't stop wondering how anyone actually works out something is 200 million years old. That question is basically what pulled me toward wanting to study geology properly.

commonMistakes: Vague answer with no real place or object
Describing generic interest in 'nature' or 'science'
No sense of a question or curiosity that followed
followUps: How did you go about answering that question yourself?

question: Tell us about a piece of fieldwork or a geological site you've visited that stuck with you.
lookingFor: Genuine hands-on engagement with geology and evidence of real observation, not just a holiday story.

bullets: Describe what they actually did or observed, not just where they went
Show they tried to interpret or question what they saw
Reflect on what it taught them about geology as a discipline
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I did a week's placement with a local geological society mapping an old quarry face, and the part that stuck with me was how much disagreement there was among the volunteers about whether a particular layer was a fault or just weathering. Watching people argue from the same rock face using different evidence taught me that geology isn't as settled as textbooks make it look. I went home and reread the section on fault indicators just so I could follow the argument properly next time.

commonMistakes: Describing a trip with no actual geological observation
Treating it as a tourist story rather than fieldwork
No reflection on what it revealed about the subject
followUps: What would you have wanted to check or measure if you'd had more time?

question: What have you read or watched recently that developed your interest in geology?
lookingFor: Evidence of independent engagement beyond the syllabus, discussed with real substance.

bullets: Name something specific, not a vague genre
Explain one idea from it that actually stayed with them
Show it changed or sharpened how they think about geology
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Marcia Bjornerud's Timefulness over the summer, and the idea that stuck with me was how badly human timescales match geological ones, which is why we're so bad at taking slow hazards like sea level rise seriously. It made me want to understand the actual mechanisms behind those slow processes rather than just the headline numbers. I've since gone looking for papers on isostatic rebound because that's the example she uses that I still don't fully understand.

commonMistakes: Naming a title with no detail about its content
Choosing something too generic to discuss in depth
Claiming to have read something they clearly haven't engaged with
followUps: What's a question that reading left you with?

question: Can you explain the rock cycle and how the three rock types relate to each other?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic relationships and the processes connecting them.

bullets: Define each rock type by how it forms
Describe the processes that convert one into another (melting, weathering, heat and pressure)
Show it's a cycle, not a one-way sequence
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools and crystallises, sedimentary rock forms when weathered fragments or dissolved material get deposited and compacted into layers, and metamorphic rock forms when either of those gets subjected to heat and pressure without fully melting. What makes it a cycle is that any of the three can become raw material for another, so a metamorphic rock can weather into sediment, or get melted back into magma. I find it a useful reminder that nothing in geology is really permanent, just slow.

commonMistakes: Defining the three types but not explaining the processes linking them
Describing it as a strict one-directional sequence
Mixing up which processes cause which transformation
followUps: Can you give an example of a specific rock and trace one path it could take through the cycle?

question: What actually drives the movement of tectonic plates?
lookingFor: Understanding that mantle convection plus mechanisms like ridge push and slab pull explain plate motion.

bullets: Mention mantle convection as the underlying energy source
Name at least one specific mechanism such as slab pull or ridge push
Show awareness this is still an area of ongoing research and refinement
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The main driver is heat escaping from the Earth's interior, which sets up slow convection currents in the mantle. On top of that, plates are pulled by their own dense, cold edges sinking at subduction zones, which is called slab pull, and pushed a little by magma rising and spreading at mid-ocean ridges. I find it interesting that geologists are still debating exactly how much each of those mechanisms contributes, which shows the theory is still being refined even though the basic model is well established.

commonMistakes: Saying plates 'float on magma' with no mechanism
Only naming convection without mentioning slab pull or ridge push
Treating the theory as fully settled with no nuance
followUps: Why does that mean the Pacific is shrinking while the Atlantic is growing?

question: If I gave you two similar-looking minerals, how would you go about telling them apart?
lookingFor: Practical knowledge of diagnostic mineral properties and how to apply them systematically.

bullets: Name specific diagnostic tests: hardness (Mohs scale), cleavage, streak, lustre
Explain how to apply at least one test practically
Show they understand no single test is always conclusive
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start with something simple like streak, scratching the mineral on an unglazed tile, because colour alone can be misleading but the streak is usually consistent for a given mineral. Then I'd check hardness against the Mohs scale using a fingernail, a coin, and a knife as rough benchmarks, and look at how it breaks, whether it has flat cleavage planes or a more irregular fracture. Quartz and calcite are a classic pair that look alike but calcite is much softer and reacts with dilute acid, so I'd try that too if I had some on hand.

commonMistakes: Relying only on colour to identify a mineral
Naming tests without explaining how to actually perform them
Not acknowledging that some properties overlap between minerals
followUps: What would you do if two tests gave you conflicting answers?

question: How do geologists work out the relative order in which rock layers formed, without using any dating equipment?
lookingFor: Understanding of basic stratigraphic principles like superposition and cross-cutting relationships.

bullets: State the law of superposition (older layers at the bottom, undisturbed)
Mention at least one other principle such as cross-cutting relationships or inclusions
Note the caveat that layers can be tilted or overturned, so context matters
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The starting point is the law of superposition, which says that in an undisturbed sequence the oldest layers are at the bottom and the youngest are on top, because sediment simply piles up over time. You can add to that with cross-cutting relationships, so if a fault or an igneous intrusion cuts through several layers, it has to be younger than all of them. The tricky part is that layers can get folded or even flipped over by tectonic activity, so geologists also look for clues like graded bedding to work out which way is actually 'up' before trusting the sequence.

commonMistakes: Only naming superposition and stopping there
Assuming rock layers are always found flat and undisturbed
Not knowing any principle beyond 'older is at the bottom'
followUps: What would make you suspect a sequence had been overturned?

question: What makes a fossil useful as an index fossil?
lookingFor: Understanding of the criteria: short time range, wide geographic spread, easy identification, abundance.

bullets: State that it needs a short time range so it pins down a narrow window
Mention wide geographic distribution so it's useful across different sites
Add that it should be common and easy to identify
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A good index fossil is one from a species that existed for a fairly short span of geological time but spread out widely and quickly, so finding it anywhere tells you roughly when that layer formed. Ammonites are a classic example because different species evolved and died out relatively fast but were distributed across whole oceans. It also helps if the fossil is common and has a distinctive shape, otherwise geologists in the field can't identify it reliably enough to rely on it.

commonMistakes: Confusing index fossils with just 'old' or 'rare' fossils
Forgetting the geographic spread requirement
Not mentioning ease of identification
followUps: Can you think of a fossil that would make a poor index fossil, and why?

question: Why do most earthquakes happen at plate boundaries rather than randomly across the Earth's surface?
lookingFor: Understanding of stress accumulation at boundaries and the different boundary types.

bullets: Explain that stress builds where plates interact and gets released as seismic energy
Distinguish briefly between at least two boundary types (convergent, divergent, transform)
Acknowledge intraplate earthquakes exist but are far less common
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Plate boundaries are where plates are grinding past each other, colliding, or pulling apart, and all of that interaction builds up stress in the rock until it's released suddenly as an earthquake. A transform boundary like the San Andreas Fault is a good example, where plates slide past each other and get locked by friction until they slip. It's not the only place earthquakes happen, intraplate quakes do occur, but they're much rarer because there's less ongoing stress being generated away from those boundaries.

commonMistakes: Saying earthquakes 'just happen' at boundaries with no mechanism
Confusing convergent and divergent boundary behaviour
Claiming earthquakes never happen away from boundaries
followUps: Why might an earthquake at a subduction zone be more dangerous than one at a transform boundary?

question: Why do some volcanoes erupt explosively while others produce gentle lava flows?
lookingFor: Understanding of magma viscosity and gas content as the key controlling factors.

bullets: Identify magma composition (silica content) as the main control on viscosity
Link higher viscosity and trapped gas to explosive eruptions
Give an example of each type
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It mostly comes down to how much silica is in the magma, because that controls how viscous, or sticky, it is. Basaltic magma like you get in Hawaii is low in silica, so it's runny and gas can escape easily, producing those gentle, flowing eruptions. Magma that's higher in silica, like the andesitic or rhyolitic magma at somewhere like Mount St Helens, is thick and traps gas until the pressure builds up enough to blow the top off the volcano.

commonMistakes: Attributing eruption style purely to 'how much magma there is'
Not connecting viscosity to silica content
Giving no concrete example of either type
followUps: Why does that mean explosive volcanoes are often found near subduction zones?

question: If you saw the terms 'strike' and 'dip' on a geological map, what would they be telling you?
lookingFor: A solid grasp of structural geology fundamentals used in field mapping.

bullets: Define strike as the compass direction of the horizontal line on a tilted rock surface
Define dip as the angle the layer plunges below horizontal, and its direction
Explain why this matters for predicting what's underground or matching layers across an area
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Strike is the compass bearing of a horizontal line drawn along a tilted rock layer, so it tells you which direction the layer runs across the landscape. Dip is the angle the layer tips down below horizontal, measured at right angles to the strike, along with the direction it's dipping toward. Together they let a geologist predict where a layer will reappear somewhere else on the map or work out what's happening underground without having to dig, which is really the whole point of a geological map.

commonMistakes: Confusing strike direction with dip direction
Forgetting that dip is measured perpendicular to strike
Not explaining why the concept is useful in practice
followUps: How would strike and dip symbols help you predict where a layer outcrops further along a hillside?

question: What is an aquifer, and how might one become contaminated?
lookingFor: Understanding of permeable rock storing groundwater and realistic contamination pathways.

bullets: Define an aquifer as a permeable rock layer that stores and transmits water
Distinguish it from an impermeable layer, and mention porosity or permeability
Give a realistic contamination pathway such as agricultural runoff or leaking waste
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An aquifer is a layer of rock, often sandstone or limestone, that's porous and permeable enough to hold groundwater and let it flow through slowly, sitting above an impermeable layer that stops it draining away completely. It can get contaminated when something like fertiliser runoff, a leaking fuel tank, or landfill leachate seeps down through the soil and into the water table, and because groundwater moves so slowly, that contamination can spread for years before anyone notices it in a well. That's part of why geologists get involved in siting things like landfills, to avoid putting them over vulnerable aquifers.

commonMistakes: Describing an aquifer as an underground river or lake
Not mentioning porosity or permeability at all
Giving no realistic contamination source
followUps: Why might contamination in a fractured limestone aquifer be harder to predict than in sandstone?

question: What's the difference between weathering and erosion?
lookingFor: A clear distinction between breakdown in place and the transport of material away.

bullets: Define weathering as the breakdown of rock in place
Define erosion as the transport of that broken material away
Give an example distinguishing physical, chemical, or biological weathering
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Weathering is the breakdown of rock where it sits, either physically, like frost getting into cracks and expanding, chemically, like rainwater slowly dissolving limestone, or biologically, like plant roots forcing cracks apart. Erosion is a separate step where that broken-down material actually gets picked up and carried away, by rivers, wind, ice, or waves. People mix the two up a lot, but the distinction matters because you can have heavy weathering somewhere with very little erosion if there's nothing to transport the debris.

commonMistakes: Using the two terms interchangeably
Only naming one type of weathering
Not explaining that erosion requires transport, not just breakdown
followUps: Can you give an example of a place with a lot of weathering but not much erosion?

question: How do geologists use rocks and sediments to understand past climate change?
lookingFor: Awareness of proxy evidence such as ice cores, sediment cores, or isotope ratios.

bullets: Name at least one specific proxy record (ice cores, ocean sediment cores, tree rings)
Explain briefly what signal it preserves, such as oxygen isotopes or layering
Connect it to why this matters for understanding current climate change
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One of the clearest examples is ice cores, where each year's snowfall gets compressed into a layer that traps tiny air bubbles, and the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the ice itself tells you roughly what the temperature was when it fell. Ocean sediment cores work similarly, using the isotope ratios in the shells of tiny marine organisms that get buried in layers over time. What I find compelling is that these give us a real record stretching back hundreds of thousands of years, which is exactly the baseline you need to judge how unusual the current rate of warming actually is.

commonMistakes: Vague answer with no named proxy record
Not explaining what signal the proxy actually captures
Missing the link to why this matters for present-day climate science
followUps: Why might tree rings be less useful than ice cores for very ancient climate records?

question: Geology underpins mining, which has real environmental and social costs. How do you think about that tension?
lookingFor: Balanced, thoughtful reasoning that doesn't dismiss either the necessity of resources or the real costs of extraction.

bullets: Acknowledge society's genuine dependence on minerals, including for green technology
Recognise real environmental and social costs of extraction honestly
Reason toward a nuanced position, such as better regulation or geologists' role in responsible siting
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think there's a clean answer, because the same minerals that cause real damage when mined badly, like lithium or copper, are also essential for batteries and renewable infrastructure, so simply opposing mining doesn't really solve anything. What I think geology can actually contribute is better site selection and impact assessment, understanding groundwater flow or seismic risk before a mine is built rather than after something goes wrong. I'd rather be part of making extraction more responsible than pretend the demand for these resources is going away.

commonMistakes: Dismissing mining entirely with no acknowledgment of necessity
Ignoring the real environmental and social harms
Giving a one-line answer with no actual reasoning
followUps: What role do you think a geologist specifically can play in reducing that harm?

question: Is there a geological feature or landscape, anywhere in the world, that particularly fascinates you?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific curiosity backed by some understanding of how the feature actually forms.

bullets: Name a specific feature, not a vague category like 'mountains'
Explain roughly how it forms
Show genuine enthusiasm rather than a rehearsed textbook answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm a bit obsessed with the Giant's Causeway, those hexagonal basalt columns in Northern Ireland. They form when a thick lava flow cools slowly and evenly enough that it contracts into these near-perfect polygonal cracks, which always struck me as strange because nothing about the process is deliberately geometric, it just falls out of the physics of even cooling. I like that it's a reminder that some of the most striking-looking landscapes come from very ordinary processes happening consistently.

commonMistakes: Naming a feature with no explanation of how it forms
Choosing something too generic to discuss with any depth
Sounding rehearsed rather than genuinely curious
followUps: What would you want to check if you visited in person?

question: Fieldwork often gives you messy or ambiguous data. Can you describe a time you had to deal with that, or how you imagine you'd handle it?
lookingFor: Realistic understanding that field geology involves uncertainty and interpretation, not neat textbook answers.

bullets: Acknowledge that real field data is rarely as clean as a textbook diagram
Describe a specific approach to resolving ambiguity, such as more observations or cross-checking
Show comfort with uncertainty rather than needing a single 'right' answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: On a school geology field trip we were trying to work out the direction a river channel had migrated from the sediment structures in an old quarry, and two of us read the cross-bedding completely differently. Rather than argue over who was right, we went back and measured the dip direction of several more beds nearby to get a pattern instead of relying on one exposure, and it turned out the initial reading had just been from an unusually disturbed section. It taught me that in the field you're rarely looking for one perfect answer, you're building confidence through repeated observation.

commonMistakes: Claiming field data is always straightforward to interpret
Describing a purely classroom scenario with no field element
Not showing any actual method for resolving the ambiguity
followUps: How would you handle it if two experienced geologists genuinely disagreed on an interpretation?

question: Has a recent earthquake, volcanic eruption, or other geological event in the news caught your attention? What did you take from it?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with current geoscience news and the ability to connect it to underlying concepts.

bullets: Reference a real, specific recent event rather than a vague generality
Explain the geological mechanism behind it in their own words
Reflect on a broader implication, such as hazard preparedness or monitoring
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I followed the coverage of the volcanic activity in Iceland fairly closely, partly because it kept getting reported as 'surprising' when geologists there had actually been tracking the magma intrusion and seismic swarms for weeks beforehand. It made me appreciate how much of hazard geology is really about monitoring and probability rather than prediction in the way news headlines imply. It also made me want to understand more about how GPS and tiltmeter data actually get turned into an eruption forecast.

commonMistakes: Naming an event with no detail on what actually happened geologically
Choosing something so vague it could be any event, any year
Showing no reflection or broader takeaway
followUps: What do you think geologists could have communicated differently to the public in that case?

question: Within geology, is there a particular area you think you'd like to specialise in, and why?
lookingFor: A genuine, informed direction while showing openness to it evolving over the course.

bullets: Name a specific subfield, such as volcanology, hydrogeology, or structural geology
Explain what specifically draws them to it
Show awareness that their interest may shift once exposed to more of the course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to structural geology, the mechanics of how rocks fold and fault under stress, because it feels like the closest thing geology has to physics problems you can actually walk around inside. I got a taste of it doing some fault mapping on a residential field course last year and found the puzzle of it genuinely absorbing. I'm not locking myself into it though, I know a lot of people go in expecting one specialism and come out loving something completely different once they've tried more of the course.

commonMistakes: Naming a subfield with no explanation of the appeal
Sounding rigidly fixed on one path this early
Naming something they clearly can't discuss beyond the label
followUps: What's a question in that area you'd like the course to help you answer?

question: How does what you've learned in another subject, like chemistry or physics, help you understand geology?
lookingFor: Ability to connect geology to other science disciplines they've studied, showing real depth.

bullets: Name a specific concept from another subject
Explain concretely how it applies to a geological process
Show this connection deepened their understanding, not just a surface link
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Chemistry has been surprisingly central, actually. Learning about ionic bonding and crystal lattices in chemistry made mineral formation click for me in a way it hadn't before, because a mineral's crystal shape and cleavage planes are really just a direct consequence of how its ions pack together. It also helped with understanding chemical weathering, since knowing why calcite reacts with weak acid is just applying the same acid-carbonate reaction we covered in class to a rock instead of a test tube.

commonMistakes: Vague claim of a link with no concrete example
Naming a subject with no actual content connecting it to geology
Overstating the connection to sound impressive
followUps: Is there a geology topic you think would help you understand your other subjects better, going the other way?

question: How would you explain plate tectonics to a twelve-year-old with no science background?
lookingFor: Ability to communicate a technical idea clearly and accessibly without losing scientific accuracy.

bullets: Use an accessible analogy that's still scientifically accurate
Avoid unexplained jargon
Keep the explanation focused rather than trying to cover everything
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd tell them the Earth's outer shell is cracked into giant puzzle pieces, like a cracked eggshell sitting on top of the soft, hot rock underneath. Those pieces are moving incredibly slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow, because the hot rock underneath is stirring around like a very slow pot of soup. Where two pieces bump into each other, push apart, or scrape past each other, that's where you get mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes, so a lot of the most dramatic parts of the planet happen right at the edges of those pieces.

commonMistakes: Using unexplained technical terms like 'lithosphere' or 'asthenosphere'
Choosing an analogy that's inaccurate just to simplify it
Over-explaining until it stops sounding like a twelve-year-old could follow it
followUps: What part of that explanation do you think would still confuse them, and how would you fix it?

question: We say the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. How confident should we actually be in a number like that, and why?
lookingFor: Understanding of radiometric dating basics plus mature reasoning about scientific confidence from convergent evidence.

bullets: Reference radiometric dating, such as uranium-lead, as the basis for the figure
Explain that confidence comes from multiple independent methods converging on similar answers
Show understanding that scientific certainty is about convergent evidence, not a single measurement
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The figure mostly comes from radiometric dating, using the known decay rate of isotopes like uranium into lead in the oldest meteorite and zircon samples we've found. What actually gives me confidence in it isn't one measurement, it's that completely different isotope systems, using different elements with wildly different decay rates, keep converging on roughly the same number when applied to the oldest available material. That kind of independent agreement is usually a much stronger sign of reliability in science than any single precise-looking figure on its own.

commonMistakes: Treating the number as simply 'known' with no explanation of method
Describing radiometric dating without mentioning decay rates or isotopes
Confusing confidence from convergent evidence with false certainty from one method
followUps: What would make you doubt a radiometric date from a single sample?

question: What's the difference between a normal fault and a reverse fault, and what does each tell you about the stress in the area?
lookingFor: Clear structural understanding linking fault type to the stress regime, extension versus compression.

bullets: Define a normal fault as one where the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall, from extension
Define a reverse fault as the hanging wall moving up, from compression
Connect each to a real tectonic setting
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In a normal fault, the hanging wall, the block above the fault plane, slips down relative to the footwall below it, and that happens where the crust is being stretched, so it tells you the area is under extension, like a rift valley. A reverse fault is the opposite, the hanging wall gets pushed up relative to the footwall, which happens under compression, like where two plates are colliding. I remember it by thinking that a normal fault lets the crust relax and drop, while a reverse fault has to fight gravity to push rock upward, which only happens under real pressure.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which block is the hanging wall
Not connecting fault type to the underlying stress regime
Confusing reverse faults with strike-slip faults
followUps: What kind of fault would you expect to find at a transform boundary instead?
